newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus - EMI head hopes for EU action on joblessness.
newsitem.headline: Focus - EMI head hopes for EU action on joblessness.

text.p: The rising tide of Europe's joblessness emerged as a key concern for the European Monetary Institute on Tuesday although its president said he was not too worried that the problem would derail the euro.

Alexandre Lamfalussy, addressing what will likely be his final news conference as EMI head before he hands over to Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg in July, said divergent political responses to joblessness in the European Union regions were a cause for concern.

But he said he was "not too pessimistic" that the problems of joblessness could be rectified, " because I think all government officials I know recognise that a very substantial part of the unemployment problem is of a structural nature."

"If governments were to deal with this (unemployment) by applying similar structurally oriented policies, then I think that would not put at risk the EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) project," Lamfalussy said.
The EMI chief identified two central problems for the European jobs market -- inflexibility of the labour forces and excessively high indirect wage costs.
"These are remarkably similar in many countries," he said.

Lamfalussy was speaking at a news conference to mark the release of the European Central Bank forerunner's third annual report, which voiced stern criticism over many EU countries' failure to rein in their budget deficits as the scheduled launch of the euro in January 1999 looms.
In a foreword to that report, Lamfalussy was sharply critical of EU political responses to unemployment.

Noting that employment had barely risen in the region since the cyclical trough of 1993, Lamfalussy said: "Unemployment trends are...extremely worrisome; in my view the recent record of the Union in terms of job creation is dismal."

While overall economic growth looked set to accelerate in 1997, this would not suffice to boost employment as long as institutional rigidities on social security, working hours, contracts and collective bargaining practices remained.
